danish.title: Sjette bog (1808–10) — Kapitel 25
paragraphs: I løbet af det år efter sønnens afrejse blev fyrst Nikolaj Bolkonskijs (den gamle fyrst Bolkonskijs) helbred og humør meget værre. Han blev endnu mere irritabel, og det var fyrstinde Mária, der som regel måtte bære hovedvægten af hans hyppige anfald af uprovokeret vrede. Han syntes omhyggeligt at opsøge hendes ømme punkter for at pine hende åndeligt så hårdt som muligt. Fyrstinde Mária havde to lidenskaber og dermed to glæder — sin nevø, lille Nikolaj, og religionen — og disse var den gamle fyrstes foretrukne mål for angreb og spot. Uanset hvad man talte om, bragte han samtalen hen på gamle pigers overtro eller forkælelsen af børn. »Du vil gøre ham« — lille Nikolaj — »til en gammel jomfru ligesom dig selv! Synd! Fyrst Andrej ønsker en søn og ikke en gammel jomfru,« plejede han at sige. Eller han vendte sig mod mademoiselle Bourienne og spurgte hende i fyrstinde Marías nærhed, hvad hun syntes om vores landsbypræster og ikoner, og spøgte med dem.

Han sårede ustandseligt fyrstinde Marías følelser og plagede hende, men det kostede hende ingen anstrengelse at tilgive ham. Kunne han være skyld over for hende, eller kunne hendes far, som hun vidste elskede hende trods alt, være uretfærdig? Og hvad er retfærdighed? Fyrstinden tænkte aldrig over det stolte ord »retfærdighed«. Alle menneskets komplicerede love samledes for hende i én klar og enkel lov — kærlighedens og selvopofringens lov, forkyndt af Ham, der kærligt led for menneskeheden, skønt Han selv var Gud. Hvad havde hun med andre menneskers retfærdighed eller uretfærdighed at gøre? Hun måtte udholde og elske, og det gjorde hun.

I løbet af vinteren var fyrst Andrej kommet til Lysye Gory og havde været munter, blid og mere kærlig, end fyrstinde Mária havde kendt ham i lang tid. Hun følte, at noget var sket med ham, men han sagde intet til hende om sin kærlighed. Før han rejste, havde han en lang samtale med sin far om noget, og fyrstinde Mária lagde mærke til, at de før hans afrejse var utilfredse med hinanden.

Kort efter at fyrst Andrej var rejst, skrev fyrstinde Mária til sin veninde Julie Karágina i Petersborg, som hun havde drømt om (som alle piger drømmer) at gifte med sin bror, og som på det tidspunkt var i sorg over sin egen bror, der var faldet i Tyrkiet.
Sorg er, som det synes, vores fælles lod, min kære, ømme veninde Julie.

Dit tab er så frygteligt, at jeg kun kan forklare det som et særligt forsyn fra Gud, der, fordi Han elsker dig, ønsker at prøve dig og din fortræffelige mor. Åh, min veninde! Religionen, og religionen alene, kan — jeg vil ikke sige trøste os — men redde os fra fortvivlelse. Religionen alene kan forklare os, hvad mennesket uden dens hjælp ikke kan fatte: hvorfor, af hvad grund, gode og ædle væsener, der er i stand til at finde lykke i livet — som ikke blot ikke skader nogen, men er nødvendige for andres lykke — kaldes bort til Gud, mens grusomme, unyttige, skadelige personer, eller sådanne som er en byrde for sig selv og andre, får lov at leve. Det første dødsfald, jeg oplevede, og som jeg aldrig vil glemme — min kære svigerindes — efterlod det indtryk på mig. Ligesom du spørger skæbnen, hvorfor din strålende bror måtte dø, spurgte jeg, hvorfor den engel Lise, som ikke blot aldrig gjorde nogen fortræd, men i hvis sjæl der aldrig var en uvenlig tanke, måtte dø. Og hvad tror du, kære veninde? Fem år er gået, og allerede begynder jeg med min ringe forstand klart at se, hvorfor hun måtte dø, og på hvilken måde den død blot var et udtryk for Skaberens uendelige godhed, hvis enhver handling, skønt generelt uforståelig for os, kun er et udtryk for Hans uendelige kærlighed til sine skabninger. Måske, tænker jeg ofte, var hun for englelig uskyldig til at have styrke til at opfylde alle en mors pligter. Som ung hustru var hun dadelfri; måske kunne hun ikke have været det som mor. Som det er, har hun ikke blot efterladt os, og især fyrst Andrej, med de reneste savn og minder, men sandsynligvis vil hun dér modtage en plads, jeg ikke tør håbe på for mig selv. Men for ikke kun at tale om hende alene: den tidlige og forfærdelige død har haft den mest velgørende indflydelse på mig og min bror trods al vores sorg. Dengang, i tabets øjeblik, kunne disse tanker ikke forekomme mig; jeg ville da have afvist dem med rædsel, men nu er de meget klare og sikre. Jeg skriver alt dette til dig, kære veninde, blot for at overbevise dig om den evangeliske sandhed, der er blevet mit livsprincip: ikke et eneste hår på vores hoveder falder uden Hans vilje. Og Hans vilje styres kun af uendelig kærlighed til os, og derfor er hvad end der rammer os til vores bedste.

Du spørger, om vi vil tilbringe næste vinter i Moskva. Trods mit ønske om at se dig tror jeg det ikke og ønsker det heller ikke. Du vil blive overrasket over at høre, at grunden er Buonaparte! Sagen er den: min fars helbred forværres mærkbart, han kan ikke tåle nogen modsigelse og bliver irritabel. Denne irritabilitet er, som du ved, især rettet mod politiske spørgsmål. Han kan ikke udholde tanken om, at Buonaparte forhandler på lige fod med alle Europas suveræner og især med vores egen, den store Katarinas barnebarn! Som du ved, er jeg ganske ligeglad med politik, men af min fars bemærkninger og hans samtaler med Mikhail Ivánovitj ved jeg alt, hvad der foregår i verden, og især om de æresbevisninger, Buonaparte modtager, som kun her på Lysye Gory i hele verden, synes det, ikke anerkendes som en stor mand, endsige som Frankrigs kejser. Og min far kan ikke bære dette. Det forekommer mig, at det hovedsageligt er på grund af sine politiske synspunkter, at min far er modvillig mod at tale om at rejse til Moskva, for han forudser de sammenstød, der ville følge af hans måde at udtrykke sine meninger på uden hensyn til nogen. Al den gavn, han kunne have af en kur, ville han miste som følge af stridigheder om Buonaparte, der ville være uundgåelige. Under alle omstændigheder vil det snart blive afgjort.

Vores familieliv går i den gamle gænge bortset fra min bror Andrejs fravær. Han har, som jeg skrev til dig før, forandret sig meget i den seneste tid. Efter sin sorg er han først i år rigtig kommet til sig selv igen. Han er igen blevet, som jeg kendte ham som barn: venlig, kærlig, med det hjerte af guld, som jeg ikke kender mage til. Han har indset, forekommer det mig, at livet ikke er forbi for ham. Men sammen med denne sjælelige forandring er han fysisk blevet meget svagere. Han er blevet tyndere og mere nervøs. Jeg er bekymret for ham og glad for, at han tager denne rejse til udlandet, som lægerne for længst anbefalede. Jeg håber, den vil helbrede ham. Du skriver, at man i Petersborg omtaler ham som en af de mest aktive, dannede og dygtige unge mænd. Tilgiv min forfængelighed som slægtning, men jeg har aldrig tvivlet på det. Det gode, han har gjort her for alle, fra sine bønder til adelen, er umådeligt. Ved sin ankomst til Petersborg fik han kun sin fortjente anerkendelse. Jeg undrer mig altid over, hvordan rygter flyver fra Petersborg til Moskva, især så falske som det, du skriver om — jeg mener rygtet om min brors forlovelse med den lille Rostova. Jeg tror ikke, min bror nogen sinde vil gifte sig igen, og slet ikke med hende, og det er grunden: for det første ved jeg, at skønt han sjældent taler om den hustru, han har mistet, er sorgen over tabet gået for dybt i hans hjerte til, at han nogen sinde ville beslutte sig for at give hende en efterfølger og vores lille engel en stedmor. For det andet, så vidt jeg ved, er den pige ikke af den slags, der kunne behage fyrst Andrej. Jeg tror ikke, han ville vælge hende til hustru, og ærligt talt ønsker jeg det ikke. Men jeg løber for langt og er ved enden af mit andet ark. Farvel, min kære veninde. Måtte Gud bevare dig i sin hellige og mægtige varetægt. Min kære veninde, mademoiselle Bourienne, sender dig kys.

english.title: Book Six (1808 - 10) — Chapter 25
paragraphs: During that year after his son's departure, old Prince Nicholas Bolkonsky's health and temper grew much worse. He became still more irritable, and it was Princess Mary who usually bore the brunt of his frequent fits of unprovoked anger. He seemed to search deliberately for her most sensitive spots in order to torment her mentally as cruelly as possible. Princess Mary had two passions and therefore two sources of joy — her nephew, little Nicholas, and religion — and these were the old prince's favorite targets for mockery and attack. Whatever the topic of conversation, he would steer it around to the superstitions of old maids or the pampering and spoiling of children. "You want to turn him" — little Nicholas — "into an old maid like yourself! A pity! Prince Andrew wants a son, not an old maid," he would say. Or, turning to Mademoiselle Bourienne, he would ask her in Princess Mary's presence how she liked their village priests and icons, and would joke about them.

He continually hurt Princess Mary and tormented her, but it cost her no effort to forgive him. Could he really be to blame? Could her father, whom she knew loved her in spite of everything, truly be unjust? And what is justice? The princess never dwelt on that proud word "justice." All the complex laws of humanity were reduced for her into one clear and simple law — the law of love and self-sacrifice taught by Him who lovingly suffered for mankind though He Himself was God. What did she have to do with the justice or injustice of other people? She had to endure and love, and that is what she did.

During the winter Prince Andrew had come to Bald Hills and had been gay, gentle, and more affectionate than Princess Mary had known him in a long time. She felt that something had happened to him, but he told her nothing about his love. Before he left he had a long conversation with his father about something, and Princess Mary noticed that before his departure they were dissatisfied with one another.

Soon after Prince Andrew's departure, Princess Mary wrote to her friend Julie Karagina in Petersburg — the one she had dreamed, as all girls do, of marrying to her brother — who was at that time in mourning for her own brother, killed in Turkey.
Sorrow, it seems, is our common lot, my dear, tender friend Julie.

Your loss is so terrible that I can only explain it as a special act of God's providence — He who, loving you, wishes to try you and your excellent mother. Oh, my friend! Religion, and religion alone, can — I will not say comfort us — but save us from despair. Religion alone can explain what without its help we cannot comprehend: why kind and noble people who could find happiness in life — who harm no one and are necessary to the happiness of others — are called away to God, while cruel, useless, harmful people, or those who are a burden to themselves and to everyone around them, are left alive. The first death I ever witnessed, one I shall never forget — that of my dear sister-in-law — left that impression on me. Just as you ask fate why your wonderful brother had to die, so I asked why that angel Lise, who never wronged anyone and in whose soul there was never an unkind thought, had to die. And what do you think, dear friend? Five years have passed since then, and I, with my small understanding, am beginning to see clearly why she had to die, and in what way that death was an expression of the infinite goodness of the Creator, whose every action, though generally incomprehensible to us, is nothing but a manifestation of His infinite love for His creatures. Perhaps, I often think, she was too angelically innocent to have the strength to fulfill all a mother's duties. As a young wife she was irreproachable; perhaps she could not have been so as a mother. As it is, she has not only left us — and particularly Prince Andrew — with the purest memories and regrets, but she will likely receive there a place I dare not hope for myself. But to speak not of her alone — that early and terrible death has had the most beneficial influence on me and on my brother despite all our grief. Then, at the moment of our loss, these thoughts would never have occurred to me; I would have dismissed them with horror. But now they are very clear and certain. I write all this to you, dear friend, only to convince you of the Gospel truth which has become the guiding principle of my life: not a single hair of our heads will fall without His will. And His will is governed only by infinite love for us, and so whatever happens to us is for our good.

You ask whether we shall spend next winter in Moscow. Despite my wish to see you, I don't think so and don't want to. You will be surprised to hear that the reason is Bonaparte! Here is why: my father's health is growing noticeably worse; he cannot tolerate any contradiction and is becoming irritable. This irritability is, as you know, directed mainly at political matters. He cannot endure the idea that Bonaparte is negotiating on equal terms with all the sovereigns of Europe, and especially with ours, the grandson of the Great Catherine! As you know, I am quite indifferent to politics, but from my father's conversations and his talks with Michael Ivanovich I know everything that goes on in the world, and especially about the honors being heaped on Bonaparte — who, it seems, is accepted everywhere in the world as a great man and even Emperor of France, everywhere except at Bald Hills. And my father cannot bear it. It seems to me that it is mainly because of his political views that my father is reluctant to speak of going to Moscow; for he foresees the confrontations that would result from his habit of expressing his opinions without regard for anyone. Any benefit he might get from medical treatment he would lose in the arguments about Bonaparte that would be unavoidable. In any case the matter will be decided very soon.

Our family life goes on as before, except for my brother Andrew's absence. He, as I wrote to you before, has changed very much of late. After his grief, it was only this year that he truly recovered his spirits. He has become again as I knew him when we were children: kind, affectionate, with that heart of gold for which I know no equal. He has realized, it seems to me, that life is not over for him. But along with this inner change he has grown physically much weaker. He has become thinner and more nervous. I worry about him and am glad he is taking this trip abroad that his doctors have long recommended. I hope it will restore his health. You write that in Petersburg he is spoken of as one of the most active, cultivated, and capable of the young men. Forgive my family pride, but I never doubted it. The good he has done for everyone here, from his peasants to the gentry, is incalculable. On his arrival in Petersburg he received only his due. I am always amazed at the way rumors fly from Petersburg to Moscow, especially false ones such as the one you mention — that my brother is engaged to the little Rostova. I do not think my brother will ever marry again, and certainly not her; and this is why: first, I know that though he rarely speaks of the wife he lost, the grief of that loss has gone too deep in his heart for him ever to give her a successor and our little angel a stepmother. Second, as far as I know, that girl is not the kind who could please Prince Andrew. I do not think he would choose her for a wife, and frankly I would not wish it. But I am going on too long and am at the end of my second sheet. Goodbye, my dear friend. May God keep you in His holy and mighty care. My dear friend Mademoiselle Bourienne sends you kisses.
